title: Rabi' al-Awwal
hook: the month of the Prophet's birth and death, marked differently by different Muslims

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashura: a Sunni fast for Musa's rescue, and a Shia day of mourning for Husayn. Your line: two ways of keeping it. Did you shape your one gentle question? Today, another month that Muslims keep in more than one way. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

Someone asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about fasting on Mondays. It's a practical question. Why that day? His answer, kept in Sahih Muslim, isn't practical at all. In paraphrase: that is the day I was born, and the day revelation came down to me. So he marked the day of his own birth, every week, with a fast. Some Muslims recall that answer when a particular month comes round each year: Rabi' al-Awwal, the month tradition gives for his birth, and for his death.
screen: `WHY FAST ON MONDAYS?` → `THE DAY I WAS BORN.` → `A MONTH REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Start with the month itself. The Qur'an never gives the date of his birth. The early biographies place it in Rabi' al-Awwal, and tradition places his death in the same month. Al-Bukhari keeps a report that he died on a Monday, the day of the week he was born. The exact day of the month is remembered differently by different communities. So it's a month with a birth and a death folded inside it. Second, the celebration, as those who keep it explain it. Some Muslims mark his birth in this month with a gathering called the mawlid. People recite the Qur'an, sing poems in his praise, tell the story of his life, and share food. Those who keep it describe it as joy at a mercy, and point to a verse in surah al-Anbiya, in Pickthall's words: "We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples." If Allah sent a mercy, they say, it's right to be glad of it, and they point to the Monday fast as his own way of marking the day. Third, the restraint, as those who hold back explain it. Other Muslims, and some scholars, hold that his birth shouldn't be set apart as a festival, because the Prophet and his companions didn't do so, and they keep the month like any other, and say their love for him is no less. For them, the way to honor him is to follow his example every day, and they point to surah al-Ahzab: "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example." Fourth, notice what both sides share. Nobody here is arguing about whether to love him. They differ about how to show it. One holds a gathering. The other holds the line. Both say they're doing it for him.
screen: `A BIRTH AND A DEATH IN ONE MONTH.` · `THE MAWLID: JOY AT A MERCY.` · `HOLDING BACK: FOLLOW HIM DAILY.` · `BOTH SAY: FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: read about his life. Not right now in a book, but in memory first. Settle, and breathe. Bring back one scene from his life you've met on this path. Him serving his family at home. Him tending sheep. Him weeping at his son's death. Hold that one scene for a few breaths, as clearly as you can. Then choose one part of his life you don't know yet, and decide to read about it this month in a biography, a sira. If you pray, you can send blessings on him the way Muslims do when his name is said. The bell holds the time.
Rabi' al-Awwal. The month tradition gives for the Prophet's birth and his death, marked with a mawlid by some Muslims and kept like any other month by others. Today's word.
Your line: his month. Today, read one page about his life, from any biography you trust, and notice one detail you didn't know. Tomorrow, Rajab and Sha'ban. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Some Muslims mark the Prophet's birth in Rabi' al-Awwal with a mawlid gathering of Qur'an recitation, poetry in his praise, stories of his life and shared food; others, following scholars who hold it shouldn't be set apart as a festival, keep the month like any other and honor him by following his example.

it doesn't; the month comes from the early biographies and tradition.
in Sahih Muslim, he linked his Monday fast to his birth
that is the day I was born, and the day revelation came to me.
Muslims who don't celebrate the mawlid love him less
they differ about how to show love, not whether to love him.

fork.setup: someone asks the Prophet why he fasts on Mondays. what does he say?
options: it's the day I was born, and the day revelation came to me.
it's the easiest day of the week to fast.
because Ramadan began on a Monday.
fork.reveal: in Sahih Muslim, he ties the Monday fast to his own birth and to the coming of revelation.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the month tradition gives for the Prophet's birth.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rabi' al-Awwal is the month all Muslims celebrate the Prophet's birthday.
what it means: the month tradition gives for his birth and death; some keep a mawlid, others keep the month like any other, and both say it's for love of him.
what a scholar hears: the Monday fast in Sahih Muslim, the Monday of his death in al-Bukhari, and the old debate over whether the mawlid is a praiseworthy practice.

notes: Both the pro-mawlid and the cautious positions should be checked by scholars from each side for fair wording.
Confirm Bukhari 1387 (Abu Bakr asks 'A'ishah on which day the Prophet died: Monday) and Muslim 1162 (the Monday question).
Birth and death in Rabi' al-Awwal are presented as tradition and the early biographies; no day of the month is given because communities differ.
The practice mentions 'him tending sheep' and 'weeping at his son's death', from days 1333 and 1345; confirm those scripts carry them.
Editor pass: removed 'giving thanks' (not in Muslim 1162) and the general 'Muslims remember'; the cautious position now speaks for its own love rather than the narrator measuring it.
